question: Which of the following is a function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?

options.B: phagocytoses rod and cone inner segments

explanation: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a single layer of cells that lies between the retina and Bruch's membrane. The RPE is continuous with the pigment epithelium of the ciliary body. Each RPE cell has an apical portion whose villous processes envelop the outer segments of the photoreceptor cells. The lateral surfaces of adjacent RPE cells are joined by tight junctional complexes near the apices. These junctional complexes form the outer retinal blood-ocular barrier. Some of the functions of the RPE include: • Forms the outer blood-ocular barrier • Maintains the subretinal space • Absorbs light • Phagocytoses rod and cone outer segments • Participates in retinal and polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism (e.g. vitamin A metabolism -- the RPE generates 11-cis-retinaldehyde for the visual cycle) • Heals and forms scar tissue.

question: What layer of the retina shown above contains cells that project to the magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular cell subtypes of the lateral geniculate nucleus?
explanation: Magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular describe three subtypes of neurons located in the lateral geniculate nucleus which receive projections from the ganglion cell layer (layer C) of the retina. Magnocellular "M cells" have large diameter axons, subserve a larger area of the visual field, and are more sensitive to light and motion than parvocellular "P cells." M cells therefore play more of a role in dim lighting conditions. P cells make up about 80% of ganglion cells, are concentrated in the central retina, have smaller-diameter axons, serve a smaller area of the visual field, and play more of a role in color and acuity. Koniocellular ganglion cells were the last cells to be recognized and are thought to play an important role in blue / yellow discrimination. Koniocellular ganglion cells are also believed to be the first affected by glaucoma. This theory ties into using short wavelength automated perimetry (SWAP) to detect early glaucoma. SWAP is essentially analogous to a Humphrey visual field with a blue stimulus on a yellow background. Most modern Humphrey visual field machines can perform SWAP. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer, layer B is the nerve fiber layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer.

explanation: The outer blood-ocular barrier is formed by the junctional complexes between the apices of the retinal pigment epithelial cells. These complexes are also known as "zonulae occludentes." question: The fovea contains approximately what percentage of total retinal cone photoreceptor cells?
explanation: Approximately 90% of the total population of cone photoceptor cells exist outside of the fovea. Although it is composed of cones (no rods) and processes of Muller cells, the fovea contains only 10% of the total cone photoreceptor cell population in the retina. There are almost no cones in the retinal periphery. The density of cones within the fovea may exceed 140,000 cones/mm2. Cone photoreceptors in the fovea have a 1-to-1 relationship with bipolar cells and retinal ganglion cells which allows the fovea to produce fine visual acuity. These densely- packed cones are predominantly red-green sensitive. In contrast, the region of the retina with the greatest density of rods is extrafoveal in a ring 20 degrees surrounding fixation with a maximum density of approximately 160,000 rods/mm2. Although rod density is high in this area, visual acuity is not as fine because of summation of multiple rod responses in each receptive field (i.e. not a 1-to1 relationship).

question: Which part of the eye acts as a "heat sink" to remove thermal energy from light absorption?
explanation: The choroid has a very rapid blood flow and thus acts as a heat sink to prevent thermal energy buildup from light absorption. In fact, the choroid has the highest blood flow of any human tissue. The pathway of bloodflow in and out of the choroid is: • Blood enters the choroid via the posterior ciliary arteries. • The blood goes from an outer layer of large-caliber choroidal vessels (Haller layer) to an inner layer of smaller-diameter vessels (Sattler layer). This helps to reduce the arterial pressure of the choroid. • The blood then passes further inward through the choriocapillaris. • The blood is then collected in venules into collecting channels of the vortex veins. Most eyes have 4 to 5 vortex veins which exit the eye at or posterior to the equator. • The vortex veins drain into the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins. Other fun facts about this area: • The venous blood exiting the choroid has a very high oxygen tension. Thus, the retinal pigment epithelial cells (which are adjacent to the choroid) have an increased risk of oxidative damage.

question: Which of the following is defined histologically as the area of the retina where the inner nuclear layer (INL) and ganglion cell layer (GCL) are absent?
explanation: The foveola is defined histologically as the central floor of the fovea where the INL and GCL are absent. Clinically, the foveola is defined as the area within the fovea, approximately 0.35 mm in diameter, which corresponds to the foveal avascular zone. The macula is defined histologically as the area of the posterior retina with 2 or more ganglion cell layers. The fovea is defined histologically as the depression in the inner retinal surface where the photoreceptor layer consists entirely of cones. The umbo is defined histologically as the central concavity of the floor of the foveola.

The macula can be defined in different ways; histologically it is the region of the retina where the ganglion cell layer contains 2 or more layers of cells. On a more gross anatomic basis, the macula is considered to be the area of the retina located temporal to the optic nerve and between the superior and inferior temporal arcades. Still others define the macula lutea, or "yellow spot" (a more distinguished name for the macula), as the portion of the posterior retina containing yellow xanthophyll pigment. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer, layer B is the nerve fiber layer, layer C is the ganglion cell layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer.

question: Which layer, shown on the OCT macula above, contains the first-order neuronal cell bodies in the visual pathway?
explanation: Layer denoted by“C” is the inner nuclear layer. The visual pathway extends from the retina to the visual cortex within the occipital lobe of the brain. While photoreceptor cells transduce light into an electrical stimulus, they are not technically considered “neurons” of the visual pathway. Per BCSC retina, the first-order neuron of the visual pathway is the bipolar cell whose cell body resides within the inner nuclear layer of the retina. The second-order neuron of the visual pathway is the ganglion cell whose cell body resides within the ganglion cell layer of the retina (layer "B"). Bipolar cells and ganglion cells synapse in the inner plexiform layer. The axons of ganglion cells traverse the retinal nerve fiber layer (layer "A") until they converge to form the optic nerve. Ganglion cell axons travel from the optic nerve to the optic chiasm where more than half (~55%) decussate to the contralateral optic tract. Next, ganglion cell fibers within the optic tract terminate on third-order neurons whose cell bodies reside within the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). LGN neuronal axons travel along the optic radiations to terminate within the visual cortex of the occipital lobe of the brain. Note that a portion of the ganglion cell population (so-called “pupillomotor fibers”) do NOT synapse in the LGN but instead, are diverted from the optic tract to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain. These pupillomotor fibers function as part of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex response pathway. Because of the asymmetric decussation of ganglion cells (including pupillomotor fibers) at the optic chiasm, a lesion of the optic tract causes a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. Some common mnemonics to help remember where cell bodies and synapses between cells are located within the retina: • Inner plexiform synaptic connections: “Cells In a BAG”. Inner plexiform layer --> Bipolar cells, Amacrine cells, and Ganglion cells. • Inner nuclear layer cell bodies: "Big HAM”. Bipolar, Horizontal, Amacrine, and Mueller cells • Outer plexiform synaptic connections: “PHiBers Out”. Photorecepters, horizontal cells, bipolar cells --> Outer plexiform layer.

Per BCSC retina, retinal tissue ranks among the highest in the body in terms of metabolic rate per gram of tissue. Not surprisingly, the choroid is the site of highest blood flow of any tissue in order to support retinal metabolism as well as remove thermal energy from absorption of light. Due to such high blood flow through the choriocapillaris, RPE cells realize the highest oxygen tension of any tissue in the body and therefore are at high risk of oxidative damage. Some high-yield nerve/artery/vein numbers to memorize: • ~20 Short posterior ciliary ARTERIES • ~10 Short posterior ciliary NERVES • ~2 Long ciliary arteries • ~2 Long ciliary nerves • ~4-7 vortex veins per eye (about 1-2 per quadrant of retina) responsible for draining the uvea (choroid, ciliary body and iris) • One (1) central retinal vein responsible for draining the inner retinal circulation.

question: Angioid streaks are thought to result from increased fragility of which of the following layers on the above optical coherence tomography (OCT)?
explanation: Structure labeled “C” is Bruch membrane. Bruch membrane is composed of 5 sublayers from innermost-to-outermost in the following order: 1. RPE basement membrane 2. Collagenous inner zone 3. Inner layer of elastic fibers 4. Collagenous outer zone 5. Choriocapillaris basement membrane Angioid streaks result from breaks in an otherwise fragile Bruch membrane which expose underlying choroidal vascular layers and may result in vision loss due to acute subretinal hemorrhage and/or choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) formation. Angioid streaks may be idiopathic or caused by one of several underlying systemic disorders including pseudoexanthoma elasticum (most common identifiable cause), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Paget's disease of bone, and sickle cell (and some other hemoglobinopathies). Causes of angioid streaks can be memorized using the well-known “PEPSI” mnemonic where the letter “I” represents idiopathic. Patients with angioid streaks should receive evaluation for the aforementioned conditions. Patients should also be instructed to wear protective eyewear and may require treatments specific for CNVM if present. explanation: This child's presentation is concerning for bilateral retinoblastoma (Rb) which occurs in approximately one-third of all Rb children. In contrast to Rb, 90% of cases of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) are unilateral. PFV is a spontaneous condition, present at birth, and there is typically no family history. Males and females are equally affected. Persistent fetal vasculature is the term that has replaced the condition referred to as "persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous" (PHPV). It is considered the most common cause of a unilateral congenital cataract. PFV's clinical manifestations can be quite varied, ranging from mild cases presenting with prominent hyaloid vessel remnants and large Mittendorf dots, to severe cases with progressive angle closure glaucoma, tractional retinal detachment, and cataract formation. Most PFV eyes are microphthalmic compared to the normal fellow eye, which is important since Rb rarely occurs in microphthalmic eyes. Another classic finding (i.e. typically found on board exams) of PFV is elongated ciliary processes that are visible through a dilated pupil. Management of PFV is difficult in severe cases and typically consists of early cataract extraction, membrane excision via vitreoretinal approaches, contact lens wear, and aggressive amblyopia treatment. question: Which of the following laser settings increases the likelihood of developing a choroidal neovascular membrane (CNV) after laser photocoagulation?
explanation: Small, not large, spot sizes increase the risk of rupture of Bruch's membrane and subsequent CNV. The basic rationale is that any factor that increases the intensity of the laser burn will increase the risk of secondary CNV. Thus, a smaller spot size concentrates the same amount of power into a smaller area (i.e. more intense burn). Other factors that would increase the burn intensity are: • longer burn duration • higher power Frequently, there is the misunderstanding that a shorter duration would result in a higher intensity laser burn. This is not true. Here is an example of how to think about this properly. If you set the laser at 200 mW with a 50 msec duration, that setting will apply that power over every interval of the entire 50 msec. This 200 mW of power is not "spread over" or diluted over 50 msec. Thus, if you increase the duration to 100 msec, the 200 mW of power is applied at every interval over that 100 msec. This results in a higher intensity of laser burn compared to if the duration was shorter at 50 msec. Q-Which of the following colors of light is most absorbed by xanthophyll pigment in the macula?

Minimally absorbs red wavelengths. Thus, you would want to avoid the use of blue wavelengths when performing laser photocoagulation in the macula. explanation: The rationale behind performing focal or grid photocoagulation prior to scatter laser photocoagulation (i.e. PRP) is that the scatter may exacerbate diabetic macular edema. Similarly, focal laser should be performed prior to cataract surgery in cases of clinically significant macular edema to prevent progression of the macular edema. On a practice management level, insurance companies will not reimburse for both focal and scatter lasers on the same day. If done simultaneously, they will reimburse only for the focal/grid laser which has lower RVUs (relative value units). In addition, if a focal is performed within the post-op period (i.e. 90 days) after the PRP, then most insurance companies will not reimburse for the focal laser since it is considered the "lesser" of the two procedures. question: The photo above demonstrates fundus changes following a therapeutic intervention. These changes reflect what type of tissue reaction?
explanation: The photograph above demonstrates typical panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) scars. Photoablation, photocoagulation, and photodisruption are all types of laser-tissue interactions. Phototermination is simply a made-up term. Photocoagulation occurs when tissue absorbs light energy delivered by a laser and converts this to heat causing tissue coagulation. Photoablation occurs when laser pulses selectively ablate small areas of tissue without harming adjacent tissue. It is much less destructive than photocoagulation. Excimer lasers use photoablation in corneal refractive procedures because it allows selective ablation of tissue without resulting in damage or subsequent scarring of adjacent corneal tissue. Photodisruption occurs when laser energy is used to rupture or explode tissue. YAG lasers used in posterior capsulotomies and laser iridotomies utilize photodisruption. Q -What is the main advantage of micropulse laser photocoagulation (versus conventional photocoagulation) in the treatment of retinal vascular diseases?

question: What is the main advantage of micropulse laser photocoagulation (versus conventional photocoagulation) in the treatment of retinal vascular diseases?

options.D: Decrease the magnitude of scotomas Laser Therapy for Posterior Segment Diseases
options.C: Higher "duty cycle" of the energy being delivered
options.B: Confinement of heat to the photoreceptors and choriocapillaris
options.A: Improved ability to visualize the laser spots

explanation: In general, laser energy is thought to induce changes in the metabolic activity and gene expression of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells that are adjacent to the burn. In turn, these RPE cells release growth factors and cytokines that control vascular leakage. Conventional laser therapy delivers this required stimulus, but with the side effect of causing permanent destruction to the nearby photoreceptors. This permanent damage can lead to visually-significant scotomas, especially when applied in the macular area. The term, "subthreshold laser therapy," describes the deliverance of laser energy below the threshold of causing permanent tissue [photoreceptor] damage. The main method that is employed to deliver subthreshold laser therapy is micropulse laser, whereby the laser energy is divided into many, short pulses of energy (e.g. 100 to 300 µs duration) with a long pause (e.g. 1700-1900 µs) between pulses. The long pause allows the target tissue to cool enough to prevent permanent damage. Thus, the main benefit of the micropulse laser is the reduction of visually-significant scotomas as a result of less thermal damage to photorecptors. Answer "A" is incorrect since micropulse laser burns are actually not visible even with fluorescein angiography or autofluorescence imaging. This "invisibility" makes it more difficult to titrate treatment and to know what part of the retina has already been treated. Answer "B" is incorrect since the goal of any laser treatment is to confine the laser energy (i.e. heat) to the RPE cells, not the photoreceptors or choriocapillaris. Answer "C" is incorrect since subthreshold lasers actually have a significantly lower "duty cycle" compared to conventional lasers. For example, a micropulse laser can have a duty cycle ~5-10% of a conventional laser. A duty cycle is defined as the amount of time that the laser is actually "on" (i.e. delivering energy). question: Q,Which of the following retinal findings places the eye at highest risk for progressing from preproliferative diabetic retinopathy to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)?
explanation: The ETDRS (Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study) found that CWS were the LEAST helpful in predicting progression from preproliferative diabetic retinopathy to PDR. The Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) found strong evidence that VB and IRMA are most predictive of the risk of progressing to PDR. explanation: An International Clinical Disease Severity Scale for diabetic retinopathy was established in 2003 and was based on the findings of the Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) and the Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS). These "standard photographs" were the ones used by the WESDR fundus photo reading center to judge the severity of retinopathy. • Severe non-proliferative NPDR -- any of the following criteria (but without any neovascularization or vitreous hemorrhage) ("4:2:1 rule") o Intraretinal hemorrhages of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 2A in all 4 quadrants; OR o Venous beading of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 6B in at least 2 quadrants; OR o Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 8A. • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) -- presence of any neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or tractional retinal detachment. o PDR with "high-risk characteristics" § Neovascularization of the disc (NVD) of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 10A. Based on presence of NVD and NVE in the right eye, we can assume that PDR is the etiology of the VH in the left eye. However, we must do our due diligence to rule out other ominous posterior segment findings such as a retinal detachment or posterior segment mass (i.e. choroidal hemorrhage, choroidal melanoma, etc.) as these can significantly impact the clinical course. What if the VH is caused by a retinal tear that has now led to a retinal detachment? Once the B-scan has confirmed no other significant posterior pathology, we can proceed based on the assumption that the VH is due to PDR and treat accordingly. Treatment with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (choice A) may be appropriate after we confirm with B-scan that the etiology for the VH is not due to other posterior segment disease such as retinal detachment or choroidal mass. Determining which agent (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, or aflibercept) to treat with for this disease is controversial and beyond the scope of the written board exams. This study demonstrated that focal photocoagulation of clinically significant diabetic macular edema (CSDME) substantially reduced the risk of visual loss by 50% (Report 1). Laser treatment also increased the chance of visual improvement, decreased the frequency of persistent macular edema, and caused minimal visual field loss.
